setter.evidence: Self-booked from a social ad the same day and by accident — 'I was clicking the nine o'clock slot to see if it was different times and it just scheduled it.' He then texted asking the price and was deferred: 'I actually texted the girl as soon as I made the decision, is this going to cost $5,000 or more? And she said, Michael, answer your questions on the call.' No human setter is identified.

prospect.name: Eddie
prospect.occupation: Quality Director for a small oil-field services company; previously ran the drilling division at Halliburton until 2023, which he left on health and stress grounds. Sits 10 to 12 hours a day, roughly 2,500 steps, five days a week plus weekend calls. Holds a degree and a master's obtained later in life.
prospect.family_status: Married. Five children aged 30, 28, 16, 13 and 10, and three grandchildren, one born the week of the call. The younger three are homeschooled and play music and act rather than doing sport. His wife shops and cooks to his dietitian's meal plan. Strongly religious — 'my main goal is my kids, you know, live for the man upstairs.'
prospect.training_background: Effectively none. Has not trained since high school football, where he weighed up to 250 lb, and describes himself as sedentary for the last 15 to 16 years. Currently walks 30 to 45 minutes most mornings at a 16 to 17 minute mile pace, roughly four hours a week, plus a few push-ups and a light three-day bodyweight routine from his dietitian. Holds a discounted gym membership at his cousin's gym and refuses to use it — 'I just don't like it. I don't like going... I don't like people either, I guess.' Owns one adjustable Bowflex kettlebell, 5 to 40 lb, bought for his wife. Has never done a kettlebell workout. Lost 40 lb through diet alone.
prospect.medical: Type 2 diabetes, diagnosed roughly 18 months ago. A1C trajectory 5.7, then 6.5, then 8.8 at diagnosis, down to 6.3 at the time of the call through diet alone. Refuses all medication and specifically refused metformin when his physician prescribed it — 'I told him there wasn't no way... I'm not getting no medicine, man.' States a general distrust of doctors, has not vaccinated his children and has had no vaccinations himself since childhood. Mildly elevated cholesterol, last measured while eating carnivore. Wears a continuous glucose monitor and uses a Hume body-composition scale. Family history of diabetes on both sides. Works with a dietitian, covered by insurance, who is a personal friend and not a physician — 'He's not a doctor, so he can't prescribe stuff' — and who placed him on unspecified mitochondrial supplements for insulin resistance. Paid $500 privately for lab markers his physician declined to order. Previously did carnivore for about a year and extended fasting for over a year.

signals: In the middle of an active health event rather than recovering from a past one — diagnosed type 2 diabetes, currently 6.3 A1C and still pre-diabetic, with the explicit aim of reversing it: 'if I could lose 10% body fat percentage, and gain muscle through this program, I'm thinking I won't have a diabetic problem whatsoever'
The diagnosis is the trigger and he names it: 'What was the wake-up call for you to make a change? I went to the doctor and had diabetes.'
Extremely high motivation and stated total commitment — 'If I commit, dude, I commit' and 'if I got to eat fricking one meal a day for the next 10 years, I'm not getting on metformin'
The archetype's warning applies exactly: easy to close and the most important to screen clinically. He was not screened at all, and he is simultaneously refusing prescribed medication
Not the_rebuilder: he is not trying to recover a former self — he never trained as an adult at all, and the fight is against a live diagnosis, not a bad season

goals.text: Reverse or control his diabetes and get his A1C from 6.3 below 5.7
Never go on medication — the single most repeated statement on the call
Lose body fat, especially visceral fat, having plateaued at 210 lb
Build muscle, which he understands raises metabolic rate and is linked to longevity
Longevity — 'physical fitness is key to the longevity of life'
More energy, having said he does not know what having energy feels like
Lead by example and leave a legacy for five children and three grandchildren
Train at home in 30 to 40 minutes without ever setting foot in a gym
Learn correct form so he is not doing the movements wrong — what he named as the standout benefit
Get to a point where he no longer has to follow an app to eat correctly

pains.text: Diagnosed type 2 diabetes with an A1C that reached 8.8 and remains pre-diabetic at 6.3
Weight stuck at exactly 210 lb for months despite strict dietary compliance — 'I hadn't lost one pound. I mean, like, I'm flat'
Sedentary for 15 to 16 years, sitting 10 to 12 hours a day with about 2,500 steps
Will not use a gym despite holding a discounted membership — dislikes the environment and the people
Has never done resistance training as an adult and does not know whether he is doing movements correctly
Long unpredictable hours, woken at 2:30am to troubleshoot, which repeatedly displaces his morning walk
Deep distrust of physicians — 'they just want you out of their office and they want to make money. And the way they do that is by prescribing medication'
Years of high-stress work he says visibly aged him while running a division at Halliburton
Strong family history of diabetes on both sides, which he attributes to shared habits rather than genetics
Louisiana food culture and social eating he finds hard to navigate
Does not know what having energy feels like — 'I probably don't know what it is like to have a lot of energy, I guess'

objections.raw_quote: Yeah, I mean, I guess the big question, right? How much does it cost? Because that's what I'm going have to talk to my wife about, of course.
objections.rep_response: Deferred the price and moved to a 1-to-10 check. When the spouse dependency was restated after the price — 'I got to have my wife's buy-in too' — it was not addressed at all. None of the scripted spouse moves ran at any point.

objections.raw_quote: Well, I mean, to be honest, I'm going to talk to my dietician about it, who's a really good friend of mine, and see if he supports it, or if he tells me, no, dummy, go do this, and you can come work out with me.
objections.rep_response: Handled better than the spouse objection and largely improvised. Asked what he would think if the dietitian said no, established the dietitian has been pushing him toward strength training anyway, and reframed the consultation as certainty-seeking: 'going to him is just about creating certainty for yourself if it's the right thing at the end of day.' Then asked what could be sent to the dietitian and answered 'Show him the videos.'

objections.raw_quote: if I do it, I'd have to sell some stock because I ain't putting it on no card... I got credit cards, but they get paid off every month, and I can't pay off a $6,000 bill in a month. I'd have to sell some stock.
objections.rep_response: Isolated it correctly as a value question rather than a capacity one — 'it doesn't sound like it's a, hey, can I actually afford it thing? It sounds like it's more of like a value' — which the prospect confirmed. No payment plan was mentioned at any point, despite the prospect describing a liquidity problem that a plan directly solves.

objections.raw_quote: I just need a way out whether it's worth the $6,000. I mean, do I get up every morning and start doing this myself? Probably won't be as easy as doing it the way you guys do it, right?... So I get that, right? That's what I need to weigh. Versus, you know, how many hours I got to work to make six grand? Is it worth the trade-off?
objections.rep_response: Acknowledged the size of the decision — 'it's not like we're buying a carton of eggs down the street' — and restated the value. Did not ask why he had not already started on his own, and did not use the prospect's own $2,500 guitar-lesson analogy, which he had volunteered as proof that video accountability works.

prospect_financials.note: Volunteered. Holds company stock he would need to liquidate, pays credit cards in full monthly and refuses to carry a balance. Recent discretionary spending includes a $19,000 car paid in cash for his 16-year-old and $2,500 on a year of guitar lessons for his 13-year-old. Says the oil field pays $125,000 to $150,000 and more. No financial-picture question was asked.

evidence: No payment and no card request. The rep never asked for payment at any point after quoting the price.
Two live dependencies remained unresolved: 'that's what I'm going have to talk to my wife about' and 'I'm going to talk to my dietician about it... and see if he supports it.'
Next step set by the rep: 'why don't I give you a call on Monday? Let me know one way or another.'

Counter-evidence, positive: rated it eight to ten, said 'If I commit, dude, I commit', named a self-imposed deadline — 'I know it needs to be pretty soon, like I need to make it probably by Monday' — and volunteered a directly analogous purchase that worked: $2,500 of guitar lessons with weekly video accountability, 'So I know it works, right? I do know it works.'

Counter-evidence, negative: the booking was accidental and he had first encountered Trevor about four hours earlier — 'I was clicking the nine o'clock slot to see if it was different times and it just scheduled it. So I said, screw it.'

Counter-evidence, negative: the decisive third party is a dietitian who is also a personal friend and whose endorsement he says would determine the outcome — 'if he supports it, I might be spending that money. Why? I trust him.'
outcome.next_step: Rep to phone on Monday 2026-07-06. Prospect to speak with his wife and with his dietitian, and to send the dietitian Trevor's videos, which was the only collateral offered.

notable.note: The most serious compliance moment in the batch occurs here. Asked what happens if nothing changes, the prospect said he would keep struggling with diabetes, and the rep answered: 'we're technically not supposed to say this because of the FDA and blah, blah, blah, blah. But I mean, the amount of people that we've had come in with diabetes, they crush the program for six months, like they don't have diabetes anymore is pretty crazy.' That is a disease-reversal claim, made with explicit awareness that it is prohibited, to a diagnosed type 2 diabetic who is actively refusing prescribed metformin, distrusts his physician, and replied 'that's I guess what I'm figuring will happen.' Nobody asked whether a clinician had cleared him for training. Separately, this prospect is the clearest ICP exclusion in the corpus — 15 to 16 years sedentary, no training since high school, was 250 lb, and openly gym-averse — and he identified the mismatch himself: 'one thing with his before and after is, though, I didn't see no fat people.' He was reassured that such clients exist but are not the ones advertised. Fourth prospect in this batch to ask how payment works and be told most people pay upfront on a credit card, this time by a man who explicitly will not carry a card balance and would have to sell stock.

quality.notes: Continuous inversion, with the prospect appearing under the device label 'Fosho pad'. The rep's turns are frequently absorbed into the prospect's long monologues and vice versa — the FDA and diabetes claim at 00:28:27, the three-pillar delivery, and the $6,000 quote all sit partly or wholly under the wrong label. The prospect speaks far more than the rep and in long unpunctuated runs, which makes label-based attribution unusable here. Every quote in the flags file was attributed by content.
